title: What is the difference between array and linked list — array has fast access by index O(1) but slow insert/delete; linked list has slow access O(n) but fast insert/delete at head O(1).
shortTitle: What is the difference between array and linked list

s1_definition.profdef: An array stores elements in one contiguous block of memory, giving O(1) random access by index but O(n) insertion or deletion in the middle because elements must shift. A linked list stores elements as scattered nodes connected by references, giving O(n) access because you must traverse, but O(1) insertion or deletion at a known position such as the head. Arrays have better cache locality; linked lists avoid costly resizing and shifting.
s1_definition.analogy: An array is like a row of numbered lockers at National Bank of India bolted side by side; Rajesh can jump straight to locker five instantly, but to squeeze a new locker into the middle every later locker must be unbolted and moved. A linked list is like a treasure hunt where each clue points to the next hiding spot; adding a new clue at the start is trivial, but to reach the fifth clue you must follow the first four.
s1_definition.oneliner: Array gives fast index access but slow middle insert; linked list gives slow access but fast head insert.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An array stores elements in one contiguous block of memory, giving O(1) random access by index but O(n) insertion or deletion in the middle because elements must shift. A linked list stores elements as scattered nodes connected by references, giving O(n) access because you must traverse, but O(1) insertion or deletion at a known position such as the head. Arrays have better cache locality; linked lists avoid costly resizing and shifting.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An array is like a row of numbered lockers at National Bank of India bolted side by side; Rajesh can jump straight to locker five instantly, but to squeeze a new locker into the middle every later locker must be unbolted and moved. A linked list is like a treasure hunt where each clue points to the next hiding spot; adding a new clue at the start is trivial, but to reach the fifth clue you must follow the first four.

**One line to remember:** Array gives fast index access but slow middle insert; linked list gives slow access but fast head insert.

sections.s2_technical:
Access is the first difference. An array element at index `i` is found by computing a memory offset from the base address, which is a single arithmetic step, so access is O(1). A linked list has no such offset; to reach the node at position `i` you start at the head and follow `i` next references, so access is O(n).

Insertion and deletion is the second difference. Inserting into the middle of an array requires shifting every element after the insertion point to make room, which is O(n), and the same for deletion. Inserting at the head of a linked list is O(1) because you only re-point one reference; even inserting in the middle is O(1) once you already hold a reference to the preceding node, though finding that node is O(n).

Memory is the third difference. An array is a single contiguous block, so it has excellent cache locality: when the CPU loads one element it pulls neighbouring elements into cache, making iteration fast. A linked list scatters nodes across the heap, so iteration suffers cache misses, and each node also carries the overhead of a reference field. However, a fixed array must be resized by allocating a bigger array and copying when it fills, whereas a linked list grows one node at a time with no copying. In Java, `ArrayList` is backed by an array and `LinkedList` is a doubly linked list; for most workloads ArrayList wins in practice because of cache locality, and you reach for LinkedList mainly when you do many insertions and removals at the ends.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India needs to look up Rajesh's transaction at a specific position in a statement instantly, which favours an array. This is exactly where array O(1) index access shines.

Problem 2 — The bank also maintains a queue of newly arriving transactions where new items are constantly added at the front, which favours a linked list. This is exactly where linked-list O(1) head insertion shines.

The code has an `ArrayBackedStatement` using a BigDecimal array for fast positional access, and a `LinkedPendingQueue` using nodes for fast head insertion. The demo times both operations conceptually and logs the results so the difference is visible.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: an array of three amounts and a linked queue with two head insertions.

Step 1 — The array holds 1000, 2000, 3000 in contiguous slots. Calling get(2) computes the address of slot 2 directly and returns 3000 in one step, demonstrating O(1) access.

Step 2 — The linked queue starts empty. addFront(500) creates a node and makes it the head. addFront(750) creates another node pointing at the 500 node and makes 750 the new head. Each insertion re-points one reference, demonstrating O(1) head insertion.

Step 3 — peekHead returns the current head value, 750, which was the most recently inserted item.

Step 4 — The two logs show the array returning its index-2 element instantly and the linked queue returning its newest head, illustrating the complementary strengths.

```

2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Linked head after O(1) inserts: Rs.750.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The core difference between an array and a linked list is how they store data and the performance trade-off that follows. An array stores its elements in one contiguous block of memory, so I can jump to any index instantly by computing a memory offset, which gives constant-time random access. A linked list stores its elements as separate nodes scattered across the heap, each pointing to the next, so to reach a particular position I must start at the head and follow the chain, which is linear-time access.

The trade-off flips for insertion and deletion. Inserting into the middle of an array forces every element after the insertion point to shift to make room, which is linear time, and deletion is the same. Inserting at the head of a linked list is constant time because I only re-point one reference, with no shifting at all.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I choose the structure based on the workload. For reading a transaction at a specific position in a statement I use an array-backed structure because the constant-time index access is exactly what I need. For a queue of newly arriving transactions where items are constantly added at the front, I use a linked structure because the constant-time head insertion avoids any shifting. The last point I always make is cache locality: because an array is contiguous, iterating it is fast since the CPU pulls neighbouring elements into cache together, whereas a linked list suffers cache misses because its nodes are scattered. That is why in practice an ArrayList usually outperforms a LinkedList for iteration even though their big-O for access looks different, and I reach for a linked list mainly when I am doing heavy insertion and removal at the ends.
